Commentary.Commentary: Welcome back for UAE's reply with the bat. The umpires and players walk out to the middle. Salman Agha leads his men out as Pakistani players take their positions on the field. UAE skipper Muhammad Waseem and Muhammad Zohaib are the openers for the hosts. And it will be Salman Mirza to open the bowling attack for Pakistan. Zohaib to face. Off we go...
... THE RUN CHASE ...

Right. The hosts have a huge total to chase down and will require their openers to start with a positive intent. They will be up against a strong pace attack of Pakistan and will have to bat out of their skins to achieve this total. The dew factor will also play a huge role - if and when it arrives. Also, FYI, United Arab Emirates have successfully chased down a total in north of 200, against Bangladesh. So, they know how to do it. But will require a stronger performance against a tough opponent this time around. Stay tuned, as the run chase is on the other side.

Pakistan's Saim Ayub is in for a quick chat. Says he is very much pleased with his performance with the ball and also points that the team performance matters most to him rather than the individual milestone. He believes that it is a very good total, and they always looked to score above par on a track like this. Lauds the aggressive intent from the batters throughout the innings. And trusts his bowler to defend this total.

Pace-offs worked well for the bowlers, and they tried to pull things back to an extent by denting through the Pakistani middle order. That was the phase when Pakistan slipped from 161/4 to 177/7. But despite wickets falling at regular intervals, the incoming batters kept batting with intent and as a result, the last 5 overs went for 64 runs. Junaid Siddique and Saghir Khan snagged three wickets each, but they were very expensive. In fact, barring the two spinners, all the seamers conceded above 10 runs per over.

The pacers couldn't quite find an ideal length on a pitch where there was just enough bounce and nip in the surface. They were either too short or wayward to Ayub, and making the full use of it, he got off to his fifty in no time. But as has been the case with Pakistan lately, they kept losing wickets just when a partnership was brewing up, which kept the UAE in the hunt. At halfway, Pakistan were 93/3. Saim Ayub's wicket didn't bring any sort of slowdown in scoring as Hasan Nawaz got in his groove to go bang-bang against an inconsistent pace attack. He, too, got off to his fifty off just 24 balls, and was ably supported by Mohammad Nawaz, who played a perfect anchor before Hasan departed.

Pakistan were rocked early when Farhan fell in the opening over, yet Saim Ayub batted with intent, taking the attack head-on. UAE turned to spin quickly, and it was Haider Ali who struck gold, prising out the big scalp of Fakhar Zaman. There was a whisper of turn on offer, just enough to keep the tweakers interested, but Saim’s fearless strokeplay kept the scoreboard moving briskly. By the close of the Powerplay, Pakistan had motored to 51 for the loss of just one.

Pakistan have managed to post a very strong total on the board, and this is the fifth occasion when 200 has been breached in Sharjah, in T20Is. The last ten overs went for 114 runs, with only three overs going below double figures. A tough outing for United Arab Emirates' bowlers overall, but they would take the positive to have at least picked up all ten Pakistan wickets.

PITCH REPORT - Bazid Khan and Salman Butt are inspecting the Sharjah pitch. Bazid says it looks similar to the one that was used in the first game. Points that it is more firm and he reckons that it will be a high scoring game. Salman stresses that if dew comes in, batting in the second inning can be an advantage. Also observes that there is a good wind, so the dew factor might not come in play.

United Arab Emirates (Playing XI) - Muhammad Waseem (C), Muhammad Zohaib, Asif Khan, Alishan Sharafu, Rahul Chopra (WK), Ethan D'souza, Dhruv Parashar, Saghir Khan, Haider Ali, Muhammad Jawadullah, Junaid Siddique.

Pakistan (Playing XI) - Sahibzada Farhan, Saim Ayub, Fakhar Zaman, Salman Agha (C), Hasan Nawaz, Mohammad Nawaz, Mohammad Haris (WK), Faheem Ashraf, Hasan Ali (In for Haris Rauf), Salman Mirza (In for Shaheen Afridi), Sufiyan Muqeem.

The captain of the United Arab Emirates, Muhammad Waseem, says that they were looking to bowl and will try to restrict the opposition within 150. Says they are going with their strengths and will try their best. Adds that they are not looking on who the opposition is, rather focusing on themselves. Mentions that the boys are eager to perform and they have a good combination of pacers and spinners. On being asked if there's any pressure on him as a leader, he denies that and says he enjoys the role in this team.

The captain of Pakistan, Salman Agha, says that they will look to do the same, score runs and put them under pressure. Reckons that the pitch will be similar to the one from the first game and will look to put the runs on the board and try to restrict the opposition. Informs that they are resting Shaheen Afridi and Haris Rauf, with the likes of Hasan Ali and Salman Mirza coming in.
TOSS UPDATE - The flip of the coin lands in favor of Pakistan and Salman Agha elects to BAT first.

These two teams have met just once before in T20Is, and that was during the 2016 Asia Cup, which was held in Bangladesh, where Pakistan cruised to a comfortable win. But that was nearly a decade ago, and the cricketing landscape has massively shifted since then. The level of competition has risen, and both sides come in with plenty to prove. We are in for a much closer contest this time around. Toss and team news coming your way shortly.

Led by the dynamic Muhammad Waseem, UAE sit at number 15 in the ICC T20I team rankings and have shown steady form in the shortest format, winning three of their last five completed matches. With the comfort of home conditions on their side, they will be confident about causing a few ripples in this tri-series. There’s enough in their recent performances to suggest they’re capable of pulling off something unexpected. Alishan Sharafu has been metronomic for the UAE with the bat, whereas the likes of Muhammad Zohaib, who was their top performer with the ball at the Pearl of Africa Cup, will be key as well. Junaid Siddique will also be one to watch out for alongside Muhammad Jawadullah.

Afghanistan did ask a few questions to Pakistan, but the visitors had enough firepower to pull through comfortably, thanks largely to their sharp bowling unit. There were encouraging signs across the board. The batting effort was well-rounded, with useful knocks from several players and a standout performance from skipper Salman Agha, who anchored the middle order with authority. On the bowling front, Haris Rauf continued to impress with his pace and precision. That said, Pakistan will be looking to assert themselves more decisively in the Powerplay, where there’s still room to tighten the screws.

This tri-series serves as a timely tune-up ahead of the Asia Cup, which kicks off next week across Sharjah, Dubai, and Abu Dhabi. For both sides, it’s a chance to sharpen combinations and settle roles before the big stage arrives. UAE will see this as a valuable opportunity to push their limits and refine their approach. Pakistan, the pre-series favourites, know the expectations are high but also understand that cricket rarely follows a script. It’s all about executing well and staying switched on.

The weekend’s here and we’ve got a cracking contest lined up. Match 2 of the UAE tri-series sees the hosts take on Pakistan at the storied Sharjah Cricket Ground. Pakistan come in riding high after a dominant win over Afghanistan and will be keen to build momentum with another strong showing. United Arab Emirates, meanwhile, will be looking to rise to the occasion and test themselves against one of the region’s heavyweights. We are glad to have you with us. On that note, hello and welcome to our coverage.

The United Arab Emirates will brace for a formidable challenge when they lock horns with a transitional Pakistan side in the second match of the T20I Tri-Series at the iconic Sharjah Cricket Stadium. This encounter promises to be a fascinating contest between a determined host nation and a cricketing powerhouse undergoing a significant overhaul in its shortest format setup. The tri-series, also featuring Afghanistan, serves as a crucial preparatory ground for all three teams ahead of the upcoming Asia Cup. For the UAE, it's a golden opportunity to test their mettle against top-tier opposition and fine-tune their combinations on home soil. The hosts, led by the dynamic Muhammad Waseem, have announced a 15-member squad that blends seasoned campaigners with promising young talent. The likes of Alishan Sharafu, wicketkeeper-batsman Aryansh Sharma, and the experienced Asif Khan will be expected to shoulder the batting responsibilities. The inclusion of uncapped all-rounder Harshit Kaushik and the return of pacer Junaid Siddique will add depth to their squad. Head coach Lalchand Rajput will be keen to see his side put up a spirited performance and capitalize on their familiarity with the Sharjah conditions. Across the aisle, Pakistan presents a revamped and somewhat unpredictable outfit. In a bold move, the selectors have opted to rest stalwarts Babar Azam and Mohammad Rizwan, ushering in a new era under the leadership of Salman Agha. This strategic shift is aimed at building a squad for the future and testing the bench strength. This move has worked out, at least in the opening match of this Tri-Series, as Pakistan notched up a convincing win over T20 specialists Afghanistan, with a strong showing in both the batting and the bowling departments. The Sharjah pitch is traditionally known to favor spinners, and as the tournament progresses, it could offer some turn. Both teams will need to adapt quickly to the conditions. For the UAE, the key will be their ability to handle Pakistan's world-class pace attack and for their bowlers to contain the explosive Pakistani batting lineup. For Pakistan, it will be a test of their new leadership and the ability of their younger players to step up and seize their opportunities on the international stage.
